titulo.texto: Rock Crystal Lapidary Work and the Cup from Tomb 7

frase_gancho.texto: A quartz cup so thin that light passes right through it.

puente_narrativo.texto: From crystal we move on to another stone that lets light through: tecali. Look for a vessel with a monkey hugging it on every side.

guion_corto.texto: Alongside gold and turquoise, the master lapidaries of Oaxaca mastered the hardest and most translucent stones in nature: tecali, obsidian, and rock crystal. The absolute masterpiece of this craft came from Tomb 7 at Monte Albán, now preserved in Oaxaca, a sister to the extremely fine vessels of white stone and crystal that you see in the display cases of this hall: a cup carved from a single block of clear, transparent quartz. Without steel chisels, Mixtec artisans roughed out and hollowed the very hard crystal using only quartz sand, water, hollow reeds, and entire months of patience.

guion_largo.texto:
This is probably the most difficult piece to make in the whole hall. Rock crystal is pure quartz, and quartz is harder than most steel knives. Now consider that the Mixtec had no metal tools for cutting stone. And yet, from a block of quartz they produced a cup with extremely thin walls and perfect symmetry.

How did they do it? With patience. First the block was roughed out with careful blows of flint; then it was worn down and polished with fine sand and other abrasives, with water and with leather. The hardest part was hollowing out the inside through the mouth without breaking the walls, which ended up very thin. It is estimated that a piece like this could take months or even years of work. One false blow and everything was lost.

When you look at these translucent stone vessels and the famous cup from Tomb 7 against the light, the material almost disappears at the edges and lets light through like ice. That was exactly what they were after: for the peoples of Mesoamerica, rock crystal was solidified water, light that had turned into stone. A dewdrop turned into an object. It is the material of purity.

It was also used for seeing. Like the obsidian mirrors, such as the one belonging to the god Tezcatlipoca, the crystal allowed one to look “to the other side”: it is thought that diviners gazed into it to read destiny. Obsidian reflects and crystal lets sight pass through, but both are ways of seeing the invisible.

And what was this cup used for? We do not fully know. One possibility is that it was used to drink sacred beverages at important ceremonies: cacao, which was an elite drink, bitter and frothy, flavored with chili, not sweet like chocolate today, or pulque, the fermented drink of the agave. You already saw in the Feather Headdress how cacao from the south traveled all the way to Tenochtitlan. Drinking from a cup like this must have seemed an almost magical act.

This cup came from Tomb 7, the one with the treasure. Think of the whole set: the Mixtec lord was buried with a gold pectoral that jingled, with the skull of an ancestor covered in turquoise, and with this cup that looked like ice. Each object was a fragment of power and memory. Whoever buried him wanted their lord to arrive in the other world well accompanied and well supplied.

The Mixtec were famous for such miniatures: they carved jade, bone, jet, and crystal in such fine detail that they seem made with a magnifying glass. This cup is the best proof. Its value lies not in its size but in the work: it is an object that fits in the palm of the hand and that tells of months of patience.

One last warning, in case the word “crystal” made you think of the famous crystal skulls of modern legends. Those are forgeries, made in the nineteenth century with modern tools. This cup, by contrast, is authentic and came from a tomb excavated by an archaeologist, with all its data. The lesson is a good one: what gives value to an ancient object is not only its beauty, but knowing where it comes from.

texto: In the lapidary display cases of the hall, observe how thin the walls of the translucent stone vessels are
Notice how light passes through the polished material without leaving any tool marks
Compare this months-long work with the neighboring pieces of jade and tecali

texto.Material: Rock crystal (clear quartz carved and burnished with abrasives)
texto.Origin: Tomb 7 at Monte Albán, Oaxaca (discovered on January 9, 1932 by Alfonso Caso; held in the Museum of the Cultures of Oaxaca)

texto.pregunta: Myth: The ancient Mexicans could not work hard materials because they had no metal tools.
texto.respuesta: Reality: They did it with sand, water, leather, and a great deal of patience. With that method they achieved works of astonishing delicacy, like this quartz cup.
